title: Education The Disruptive Educator Everyone Has an Opinion on School
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: The author -- an Australian educator who attended a Carl Hendrick professional development session -- uses the extended metaphor of a butter bell (ordered without understanding how it functions) to argue that attending school does not qualify someone to make authoritative claims about how learning works. The piece targets a widespread misconception: that personal educational experience is sufficient evidence for instructional claims. Drawing a parallel to evidence-based medicine, the author argues that individual anecdotes ('but it worked for me') are not adequate evidence that a teaching approach will work broadly, because individual success stories don't generalise to populations. The article advocates for evidence-informed practice in education, situating it within the same epistemic standard applied in medicine -- randomised controlled trials over anecdote. It ends with a pointed appeal to the cognitive science backing of evidence-informed instruction, citing Sweller (2024) on cognitive load theory.
points: * Personal educational experience -- having attended school -- confers no special expertise about how learning actually works, just as eating butter grants no expertise in designing butter bells; the gap between consumer experience and causal understanding is vast. * The 'but it worked for me' argument is logically flawed: one person having an experience is not compelling evidence that the experience caused the outcome, and individual success stories cannot be extrapolated to broader populations. * Evidence-informed educators apply the same epistemic standard used in medicine: individual variation in response to an intervention does not establish that the intervention is broadly effective -- controlled trials are required to isolate causation. * Critics of evidence-informed instruction who appeal to medical autonomy are factually wrong: cognitive load theory is grounded in replicated randomised controlled trials (Sweller, 2024) -- the same standard critics claim teachers should not apply. * Opinions on schooling are both inevitable and cheap; what is expensive and rare is the kind of careful verification of instructional claims that separates evidence-informed practice from well-intentioned but potentially harmful folk pedagogy.
quotes: Everyone has an opinion on school - or rather, what schooling should look like. Of course they do. A lot of people have been to school themselves. However, attending school does little more to qualify someone to understand how learning happens than eating butter qualifies me to design a butter bell.
One person having an experience isn't particularly compelling evidence that the thing caused the outcome.

Individual success stories are not the same thing as evidence that an approach is broadly effective. The fact that something worked for one person does not necessarily mean it is likely to work for all - or even most - students.
Just because a medication or intervention works on an individual doesn't mean that it's better for the population - and it might not even work for the same individual the second time around.
All cognitive load theory effects are based on multiple, replicated, randomised, controlled trials.
